source.title: Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey Theory

accepted.question_text: For any non-equilateral triangle T in the Euclidean plane, where T is represented by its three vertices, must every 2-coloring of all points of the plane contain a monochromatic congruent copy of T?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1 ([9]). For any non-equilateral triangle T , (i.e., the set of 3 vertices of T ), E2 2−→ T.

accepted.question_text: For any triangle T in the Euclidean plane, does there exist a 3-coloring of all points of the plane such that no congruent copy of T has all three vertices the same color?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2. For any triangle T , there exists a 3-coloring of E2 without a monochromatic copy of T .

accepted.question_text: For a collinear set in Euclidean n-space, is the known result that 16 colors suffice to color the space while avoiding a monochromatic congruent copy optimal, or can the same avoidance be guaranteed with fewer colors?

evidence.quote: For any collinear set S, it is known that with 16 colors one can avoid a monochromatic copy of L in En for all n [27], but it is an open question if this is the best possible.

accepted.question_text: Is every spherical set Ramsey, meaning that for every number of colors r there is a dimension threshold N such that every r-coloring of Euclidean N-space contains a monochromatic congruent copy of the set?

evidence.quote: It is shown in [8] that any Ramsey set must lie on the surface of a sphere (in some dimension) – we call such sets spherical. In particular, collinear sets, as pointed out above, can always be avoided with at most 16 colors in any number of dimensions. It may turn out that the Ramsey sets are very easy to describe: Conjecture 3. ($1000). Every spherical set is Ramsey.

accepted.question_text: Is every four-point subset of a circle Ramsey, meaning that for every number of colors r some sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space forces a monochromatic congruent copy of that four-point circular set under every r-coloring?

evidence.quote: A weaker conjecture is: Conjecture 4. ($100). Every 4-point subset of a circle is Ramsey.

accepted.question_text: Given a Ramsey Euclidean set X and an integer r, how can one determine or bound N(X,r), the least dimension threshold such that every r-coloring of Euclidean N-space for all sufficiently large N contains a monochromatic congruent copy of X, even in the basic case where X has two points?

evidence.quote: Recall that given a Ramsey set X and an integer r, we defined N (X, r) to be the least integer such that if N > N (X, r) then for any r-coloring of EN , there is a monochromatic X 0 ∈ Cong(X). One might go farther than asking which sets are Ramsey; given a Ramsey set and an integer r, what can we say about N (X, r)? As we’ll see below, even for the simplest nontrivial case, a 2-point set, this is a major open question.

accepted.question_text: What is the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane, that is, the minimum number of colors needed to color every point of the plane so that no two points at Euclidean distance 1 receive the same color?

evidence.quote: A unit distance graph in a metric space (X, ρ) is a graph G = (X, E) with vertex set X and edge set {x, y ∈ X : ρ(x, y) = 1}. k · k will denote the usual Euclidean norm. χ(X, ρ) will denote the chromatic number of X under the metric ρ, though we omit ρ when it is the Euclidean norm. The most widely-known problem in Euclidean Ramsey theory is probably that of determining the chromatic number of the plane, χ(E2 ). This question is attributed to Nelson (see [23], [24], and [25] for a full account), and there is a wide literature surrounding it. Despite its broad interest, the best known bounds are 4 ≤ χ(E2 ) ≤ 7.

accepted.question_text: What is the polychromatic number of the Euclidean plane, defined as the least number of colors needed to color the plane so that no single color class realizes all distances between pairs of points?

evidence.quote: Say that a set S in E2 realizes distance d if some two points x, y ∈ S are distance d apart. The polychromatic number of the plane is the least number of colors χp (E2 ) such that it is possible to color the plane with χp (E2 ) colors so that no color realizes all distances. Of course, χp (E2 ) ≤ χ(E2 ), since in the latter case no color realizes distance 1. The bounds 4 ≤ χp (E2 ) ≤ 6 are due to Stechkin and published in [21], though as with χ(E2 ), the determination of the actual number χp (E2 ) is open.

accepted.question_text: For rational n-space Q^n equipped with the usual Euclidean distance and unit-distance graph coloring rule, what is the exact chromatic number chi(Q^n) for some dimension n at least 5?

evidence.quote: The chromatic number of rational space has also been studied. In [2], M. Benda and M. Perles show that χ(Q2 ) = 2, χ(Q3 ) = 2, and χ(Q4 ) = 4. The authors pose some problems in their conclusion: try to determine χ(Qn ) for some n ≥ 5 (in [4], K. B. Chilakamarri shows that χ(Q5 ) ≥ 6)

accepted.question_text: If X is an algebraic extension of the rationals, what is the chromatic number of the two-dimensional space X^2 under the usual Euclidean unit-distance coloring rule?

evidence.quote: The authors pose some problems in their conclusion: try to determine χ(Qn ) for some n ≥ 5 (in [4], K. B. Chilakamarri shows that χ(Q5 ) ≥ 6), or try to find χ(X 2 ) where X is some algebraic extension of Q, perhaps Q[ 2].

accepted.question_text: Which graphs can be represented as unit distance graphs in the Euclidean plane, meaning that their vertices can be embedded as points in the plane so that graph edges correspond exactly to pairs of points at distance 1?

evidence.quote: The question of which graphs are unit distance graphs in E2 is also open. For instance, it is easy to see that the graph K4 cannot be a unit distance graph in E2 , but it is not known if any particular subgraphs are excluded. In [3] a problem is posed: must every bipartite graph that is not a unit distance graph contain K2,3 as a subgraph? The answer is no: it is not very difficult to show that the 5-dimensional hypercube, Q5 , with all 16 of its space diagonals attached, is a counterexample.

accepted.question_text: Must every bipartite graph that is not representable as a unit distance graph in the Euclidean plane contain K_{2,3} as a subgraph?

evidence.quote: In [3] a problem is posed: must every bipartite graph that is not a unit distance graph contain K2,3 as a subgraph? The answer is no: it is not very difficult to show that the 5-dimensional hypercube, Q5 , with all 16 of its space diagonals attached, is a counterexample.

accepted.question_text: Among Lebesgue measurable subsets S of Euclidean n-space with no two points at Euclidean distance 1, how large can the density of S be?

evidence.quote: Finally, we ask a basic question about unit distances in the plane: how dense can a Lebesgue measurable set S be in En if it avoids unit distance?

accepted.question_text: What is the chromatic number of the graph on the Euclidean plane in which two points are adjacent exactly when their Euclidean distance is an odd integer?

evidence.quote: For A ⊆ R, let GA (En ) be the graph in En with vertex set En and edge set {x, y ∈ En : kx − yk ∈ A}. Very recently Ardal, Maňuch, Rosenfeld, Shelah and Stacho have shown in [1] that if we let X be the set of all odd integers, then χ(GX (E2 )) ≥ 5, but the current upper bound on this number is the trivial bound ℵ0 .

accepted.question_text: For d greater than 1 and Euclidean n-space, what is the chromatic number of the graph G_[1,d](E^n) whose vertices are all points of E^n and whose edges join pairs of points whose Euclidean distance lies in the interval [1,d]?

evidence.quote: In related work, L. Ivanov has considered the chromatic number of G[1,d] (En ) for d > 1 [12]. For this generalization of the unit distance graph, very little is currently known.

trace.notes: Normalized the input as the zbMATH document URL https://zbmath.org/5828017. The zbMATH REST API identified document 5828017 as Ron Graham and Eric Tressler, Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey theory, DOI 10.1007/978-0-8176-8092-3_7.

The DOI landing page on Springer was subscription-preview metadata rather than full technical text. Exact-title search found an author-hosted PDF at https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/10_14_euclid.pdf, but local curl could not resolve the host and the web reader did not expose the PDF body. The exact-title Paperzz HTML page matched the title and authors and exposed the full problem text, so it was used as the readable primary extraction source.
